content: High-volume, low-touch formation agents. No advisory. No structuring. No relationship. The client gets an entity, not a strategy.
What They Provide — and What They Don't

These are the high-volume, low-touch platforms — firms like Ocra Worldwide, Offshore Company Corp, and dozens of jurisdiction-specific formation agents. They offer company formation as a transactional product: select a jurisdiction, fill in a form, pay online, receive your certificate. What they provide: speed. A BVI company in 48 hours. A UAE freezone entity in a week. What they don't provide: any advisory on whether that jurisdiction is actually right for the client's specific situation. No structuring analysis. No tax optimization. Minimal post-formation compliance support. No banking introductions. No cross-border coordination. No trust or licensing capability. The client gets an entity, not a strategy.

For a mass incorporator, formation is the product — the entire product. Advisory, compliance support, banking introductions, and ongoing corporate governance are either absent entirely or offered as perfunctory add-ons that exist to marginally increase average order value. The business is built around processing volume, not understanding clients. The founder who needs a holding company for a future Series B with a US lead investor receives the same output as the freelancer registering a single-purpose trading entity. The platform cannot distinguish between the two because it was never designed to ask.

Mass incorporators live and die by lead generation. They spend heavily on Google Ads, SEO content farms, affiliate marketing, and comparison platforms. Customer acquisition cost is relatively low per transaction ($50–$200) but the lifetime value is equally low because the relationship is transactional. There is no stickiness. Once the company is formed, the client has no reason to return. The mass incorporator must continuously spend to acquire new clients because the renewal and cross-sell dynamics are virtually nonexistent. This creates a perpetual dependency on marketing spend — the moment the ad budget stops, the pipeline dries up. Growth is linear, tied to spend. It does not compound.

For a founder who simply needs a shelf company for a single, static purpose, this tier works. But the moment the situation involves multiple jurisdictions, tax residency considerations, regulatory licensing, banking complexity, or any forward-looking strategic dimension, the mass incorporator model breaks down entirely. The client ends up paying more in the long run — hiring separate lawyers, accountants, and compliance officers to retroactively fix the structuring decisions that were never made properly at formation. The cheapest option on day one becomes the most expensive option over three years.
A fundamentally different organizational identity — not a midpoint on a pricing spectrum, but a singular focus that creates compounding advantages neither tier can replicate.

Boyar occupies the strategic gap between Tier 1 and Tier 3 — and this positioning is not a compromise, not a midpoint on a pricing spectrum, and not an attempt to be slightly better than Tier 1 or slightly cheaper than Tier 3. It is a fundamentally different organizational identity that creates advantages neither tier can replicate. The distinction begins with what the firm exists to do. Mass incorporators exist to process formations. Legacy firms exist to practice law, manage pensions, or run enterprise operations — with structuring as one capability among many. Boyar exists to do one thing: build the most rigorous, most intimate, most globally capable boutique cross-border structuring and advisory practice in the market. Every dollar of investment, every hour of the founder's attention, every technology decision, every hire, every partnership — all of it is directed toward this singular purpose.
not a transaction and not a subsidiary service.

Cross-border structuring, corporate formation, licensing advisory, trust services, banking introductions, fund administration, and citizenship planning are not subsets of something else at Boyar. They are not a department within a larger organism. They are the organism. This singular focus creates compounding advantages that are invisible in Year 1 but transformative by Year 5. When corporate structuring is your entire business, you invest differently. You build jurisdiction comparison frameworks because that's your core advisory tool, not a side project. You develop licensing expertise because it's a primary revenue line, not a niche offering buried in a regulatory department. You cultivate banking relationships with the intensity of a firm whose introduction capability directly determines client satisfaction.

Mass incorporators have breadth but no depth. Legacy firms have depth but it's distributed across multiple practice areas and diluted by competing organizational priorities. Boyar concentrates all of its depth into the singular domain of cross-border structuring — and delivers it with jurisdictional breadth that approaches what institutional firms offer. Boyar's vetted partners within the Boyar Network include professionals who are members of, trained at, or formerly with legacy firms. The jurisdiction specialist in Singapore may have spent a decade at a Big Four advisory practice. The trust professional in the Channel Islands may hold the same STEP qualification and regulatory standing as their counterpart at Sovereign or Dixcart. The difference is overhead, not talent — and that structural efficiency flows directly to the client as better pricing for equivalent expertise.
No Single Competitor Combines All Three

No single competitor combines boutique advisory depth, multi-jurisdictional licensing capability, and a digital-native client experience. Boyar's positioning in the intersection of all three is deliberate. Dixcart has depth but no UAE, APAC, or licensing presence. Amicorp has scale but not boutique attention. Astons has UAE presence but no structuring depth. Ocra has formation capability but no advisory at all. Rosemont has advisory quality but single-jurisdiction concentration.
Sovereign, Vistra, TMF, Appleby — institutional credibility and deep expertise, but structuring is one department among many. Invisible to the next generation of clients.

At the other end sit the established names — Sovereign Group (37 years, 20+ jurisdictions, £20B+ AuA), Dixcart (50+ years), the major offshore law firms (Appleby, Carey Olsen, Walkers, Conyers), and the large institutional platforms (TMF, Vistra, IQ-EQ). These firms charge premium rates backed by decades of reputation, deep regulatory relationships, partner-level expertise, and institutional credibility. A structure designed by Appleby or administered by Sovereign carries weight in due diligence. Their banking introductions carry genuine authority.

But here lies the structural limitation that no amount of expertise can overcome: for these firms, corporate structuring and formation is a subset of a far broader practice — not the reason the firm exists. Trust and corporate services may represent 15–25% of the firm's total revenue — one department among many. For Sovereign or TMF, corporate services remains embedded within a conglomerate of offerings — pension administration, payroll services, global entity management, HR outsourcing — where the TCSP function is one node in an enterprise-scale operational platform.

When corporate structuring is a subset of a larger practice, it receives a proportionate share of leadership attention, technology investment, and strategic thinking. The firm's most ambitious talent gravitates toward its core — litigation for law firms, enterprise operations for TMF. The structuring practice is competent, often excellent, but it is not where the firm's deepest ambition resides. The client experience reflects this organizational reality. At a legacy firm, the client is one constituent within a broader portfolio of obligations. The partner who signs the engagement letter may oversee 200 active client relationships. The compliance team processes KYC documentation in batches, not as individual narratives. The client receives a technically proficient structure — but one that reflects the firm's institutional defaults rather than the client's specific trajectory.

Efficiency and intimacy are not the same thing — and in cross-border structuring, it is intimacy that determines whether a client's architecture is merely compliant or genuinely optimal. A founder who is eighteen months away from a Series B, planning to relocate from London to Dubai, with a co-founder who holds a different passport and a family trust that needs restructuring for the next generation — this is not a standard template engagement. Yet at an institutional firm, it will often be treated as one, because the economics of the firm reward throughput, not depth.

Their acquisition model is the mirror image of Tier 1 — relationship-driven, almost entirely referral-based, and essentially zero-cost. These firms spend virtually nothing on traditional marketing. Client flow comes through private bankers, family offices, and wealth managers; reciprocal referrals from law firms and accountants; and long-term institutional relationships. This model produces extremely high lifetime value and near-zero acquisition cost — but it took decades to build. The second weakness is invisibility to the next generation. These firms are largely unknown to digital-economy founders and cross-border entrepreneurs who don't travel in the same circles as private bankers in Geneva and trust lawyers in Jersey. A 28-year-old crypto founder in Lisbon who needs a MiCA-compliant structure will never encounter Appleby or Sovereign in their natural information ecosystem. The referral channels that serve legacy firms are generationally bounded.

You develop licensing expertise because it's a primary revenue line, not a niche offering buried in a regulatory department. You cultivate banking relationships with the intensity of a firm whose introduction capability directly determines client satisfaction. The depth-to-breadth ratio neither tier can match. Mass incorporators have breadth but no depth. Legacy firms have depth but it's distributed across multiple practice areas and diluted by competing organizational priorities. Boyar concentrates all of its depth into the singular domain of cross-border structuring — and delivers it with jurisdictional breadth that approaches what institutional firms offer. Boyar's vetted partners within the Boyar Network include professionals who are members of, trained at, or formerly with legacy firms. The jurisdiction specialist in Singapore may have spent a decade at a Big Four advisory practice. The trust professional in the Channel Islands may hold the same STEP qualification and regulatory standing as their counterpart at Sovereign or Dixcart. The difference is overhead, not talent — and that structural efficiency flows directly to the client as better pricing for equivalent expertise. No Single Competitor Combines All Three No single competitor combines boutique advisory depth, multi-jurisdictional licensing capability, and a digital-native client experience. Boyar's positioning in the intersection of all three is deliberate. Dixcart has depth but no UAE, APAC, or licensing presence. Amicorp has scale but not boutique attention. Astons has UAE presence but no structuring depth. Ocra has formation capability but no advisory at all. Rosemont has advisory quality but single-jurisdiction concentration.

Tier 3 Legacy Firms — Structuring as Subset Sovereign, Vistra, TMF, Appleby — institutional credibility and deep expertise, but structuring is one department among many. Invisible to the next generation of clients. Examples Sovereign, Vistra, TMF Fee Range $15K–$50K+ TCSP as % of Revenue 15–25% Advisor Rotation Every 18 months Structuring as Subset At the other end sit the established names — Sovereign Group (37 years, 20+ jurisdictions, £20B+ AuA), Dixcart (50+ years), the major offshore law firms (Appleby, Carey Olsen, Walkers, Conyers), and the large institutional platforms (TMF, Vistra, IQ-EQ). These firms charge premium rates backed by decades of reputation, deep regulatory relationships, partner-level expertise, and institutional credibility. A structure designed by Appleby or administered by Sovereign carries weight in due diligence. Their banking introductions carry genuine authority. But here lies the structural limitation that no amount of expertise can overcome: for these firms, corporate structuring and formation is a subset of a far broader practice — not the reason the firm exists. Trust and corporate services may represent 15–25% of the firm's total revenue — one department among many. For Sovereign or TMF, corporate services remains embedded within a conglomerate of offerings — pension administration, payroll services, global entity management, HR outsourcing — where the TCSP function is one node in an enterprise-scale operational platform. Organizational focus determines quality of attention. When corporate structuring is a subset of a larger practice, it receives a proportionate share of leadership attention, technology investment, and strategic thinking. The firm's most ambitious talent gravitates toward its core — litigation for law firms, enterprise operations for TMF. The structuring practice is competent, often excellent, but it is not where the firm's deepest ambition resides. The client experience reflects this organizational reality. At a legacy firm, the client is one constituent within a broader portfolio of obligations. The partner who signs the engagement letter may oversee 200 active client relationships. The compliance team processes KYC documentation in batches, not as individual narratives. The client receives a technically proficient structure — but one that reflects the firm's institutional defaults rather than the client's specific trajectory. Efficiency and intimacy are not the same thing — and in cross-border structuring, it is intimacy that determines whether a client's architecture is merely compliant or genuinely optimal. A founder who is eighteen months away from a Series B, planning to relocate from London to Dubai, with a co-founder who holds a different passport and a family trust that needs restructuring for the next generation — this is not a standard template engagement. Yet at an institutional firm, it will often be treated as one, because the economics of the firm reward throughput, not depth. Invisible to the next generation. Their acquisition model is the mirror image of Tier 1 — relationship-driven, almost entirely referral-based, and essentially zero-cost. These firms spend virtually nothing on traditional marketing. Client flow comes through private bankers, family offices, and wealth managers; reciprocal referrals from law firms and accountants; and long-term institutional relationships. This model produces extremely high lifetime value and near-zero acquisition cost — but it took decades to build. The second weakness is invisibility to the next generation. These firms are largely unknown to digital-economy founders and cross-border entrepreneurs who don't travel in the same circles as private bankers in Geneva and trust lawyers in Jersey. A 28-year-old crypto founder in Lisbon who needs a MiCA-compliant structure will never encounter Appleby or Sovereign in their natural information ecosystem. The referral channels that serve legacy firms are generationally bounded.

content: 30% of Formation inquiries convert to Full Structure mandates — 4–5x the revenue at zero additional acquisition cost.

The Advisory Moat is Boyar's foundational competitive advantage. Unlike Tier 1 mass incorporators who process formations as commodity transactions, Boyar begins every client engagement with a diagnostic — analyzing the client's business model, jurisdictional requirements, regulatory exposure, tax position, and long-term objectives. This advisory-first approach produces measurable results: 30% of clients who inquire about a simple company formation ($2,500) are converted to full structuring mandates ($29,700) after the diagnostic reveals that their needs require a multi-jurisdictional solution.

The advisory moat compounds over time: every successfully executed complex structure becomes a reference case that attracts similar mandates. Clients who receive genuine advisory value become referral sources — not because Boyar asks for referrals, but because the structuring quality is visibly superior to what competitors deliver. The advisory reputation itself becomes the brand: "Boyar told me something about my structure that my previous advisor missed" is the highest-value marketing any TCSP can produce.

Every advisory engagement starts with a structured analytical framework: jurisdiction comparison across 12+ variables including tax rate, substance requirements, banking accessibility, regulatory burden, setup timeline, annual maintenance cost, treaty network, reputation index, licensing compatibility, talent availability, cost of living for relocated founders, and exit/restructuring flexibility. The client doesn't receive an opinion — they receive a decision matrix. This framework naturally surfaces cross-sell opportunities. A jurisdiction comparison for a holding company reveals the case for a separate operating entity, or exposes a mismatch between personal tax residency and corporate structure. Revenue impact by Year 3: if the framework converts 30% of Company Formation inquiries into Full Structure mandates, blended revenue per client increases from ~$5,600 to ~$9,000–$12,000 without any increase in acquisition cost.
Named-advisor model creates institutional memory that cannot be replicated. Cross-sell at 2.0 services per client generates $3M from zero-CAC expansion.

The Relationship Moat is the economic engine of Boyar's compounding model. Once a client engages Boyar for any service, the advisory relationship creates natural cross-sell opportunities — and these cross-sells have zero incremental client acquisition cost (CAC). The math: a single-service client (formation only) generates $2,500 in Year 1 and $1,750 in annual renewals. A multi-service client (formation + corporate services + banking facilitation) generates $12,000+ in Year 1 and $5,000+ in annual renewals. The cross-sell multiplier at 2.0 services per client (the Year 3 target) generates approximately $3M in cumulative revenue from zero-CAC expansion of existing client relationships.

The relationship moat is reinforced by Boyar's boutique model: the founder personally knows every client, understands their business evolution, and proactively identifies structuring needs before the client articulates them. This cannot be replicated by firms where relationship managers change every 18–24 months or where client accounts are managed by junior associates with limited advisory authority. The deepest moat in professional services is institutional memory — and Boyar's named-advisor model builds it from the first engagement.
A single $75K VASP mandate cascades into $150K–$200K in lifecycle revenue. No traditional TCSP has a dedicated licensing practice.

The Licensing Moat is Boyar's most distinctive strategic asset. No traditional TCSP has a dedicated VASP licensing practice, an iGaming licensing desk, or an EMI/MSB licensing capability. Boyar's decision to enter these verticals isn't a line extension — it's category creation. Licensing expertise is experiential, not theoretical. A VASP license application in Lithuania requires understanding of the local regulator's priorities, typical timelines, documentation expectations, capital requirements, preferred governance structures, and compatible banking partners. This knowledge builds mandate by mandate. A competitor entering this space in 2028 will need 2–3 years of mandate experience to reach the depth Boyar will have by then. First-mover advantage in licensing is real.

The licensing cascade: a single licensing mandate doesn't produce one revenue event — it produces a cascade. Company formation in the target jurisdiction (formation fee), holding company in a tax-efficient jurisdiction (full structure mandate), governance documentation and ongoing corporate services (retainer), banking introductions for the licensed entity (introduction fee), annual regulatory compliance (recurring compliance revenue), and eventual licensing in a second jurisdiction when the client's business grows. A single VASP licensing mandate at $75K can generate $150K–$200K in total lifecycle revenue when the cascade is included. Revenue impact by Year 3: 10–15 completed mandates multiplied by $150K average cascade equals $1.5M–$2.25M in total licensing-attributable revenue.
81% of HNWI inheritors plan to switch firms. Boyar is built for next-gen expectations from day one — the legacy conversion window takes 3–5 years.

The Experience Moat addresses a structural shift in client expectations. Next-generation wealth holders (millennials and Gen Z inheritors managing $83.5 trillion in transferred wealth) expect advisory services delivered with the same quality of digital experience they receive from consumer technology companies. Legacy TCSPs — operating on paper files, manual processes, and email-only communication — are structurally unable to meet these expectations without multi-million-dollar technology transformations. Boyar is built digital-native from inception: structured data pipelines, real-time client reporting, digital document management, and responsive multi-channel communication.

The experience moat compounds as client expectations continue to rise. Every year, the gap between what next-gen clients expect and what legacy TCSPs deliver widens. Boyar's technology-forward approach means the firm can adopt new tools and platforms (AI-assisted compliance monitoring, automated regulatory reporting, client communication platforms) without the legacy-system integration burden that slows Tier 3 competitors. The full transformation of a legacy TCSP to digital delivery takes 3–5 years at institutional scale. During that window, Boyar owns the experience advantage.
73 retained entities by Year 5 generating $128K+ in annual recurring revenue at 90%+ gross margin — before trust fees, corporate retainers, fund admin, or licensing compliance.

The Renewal Flywheel is the mathematical proof of Boyar's compounding model. Every entity formed, every structure established, every license obtained generates recurring annual revenue: registered office fees, annual filings, compliance monitoring, corporate secretarial services, and regulatory reporting. By Year 5, the projected entity base is 73 active entities under administration. Each entity generates $1,750–$3,500 in annual recurring revenue. At 90%+ gross margin, this creates a revenue floor of $128K+ annually that compounds as each new year adds more entities to the base.

The renewal flywheel is not automatic — it requires a deliberate retention process. Every Company Formation client gets a 90-day post-formation check-in, a 6-month review, and a 10-month renewal conversation. The cross-sell happens naturally in these touchpoints — a client who formed a company in UAE mentions they're now looking at Singapore, or needs a trust for family assets, or their startup just closed a seed round and the holding structure needs restructuring for the new cap table. The renewal isn't just an invoice — it's a relationship maintenance cycle that generates organic cross-sell at zero additional acquisition cost. By Year 5, total recurring revenue (including trust fees, corporate retainers, fund admin fees, and licensing compliance) should represent 55–65% of all revenue.
100+ vetted partners across 53 jurisdictions. Building a quality network takes 3–5 years. A new entrant cannot replicate it from scratch.

The Boyar Network is a curated ecosystem of vetted professional service partners — law firms, accounting firms, registered agents, compliance consultants, and banking introducers — spanning 53 jurisdictions worldwide. Unlike franchise networks or affiliate programs, the Boyar Network is built on bilateral quality standards: every partner is vetted against Boyar's compliance criteria (AML/CFT procedures, professional indemnity insurance, regulatory standing, reference checks), and every partner's work is quality-reviewed by Boyar before delivery to the end client.

The network creates a geographic moat: a new entrant attempting to replicate Boyar's multi-jurisdictional capability would need to identify, vet, negotiate terms with, and operationally integrate 100+ partners across 53 jurisdictions — a process that takes years of active relationship building. The network also generates deal flow: as network partners become familiar with Boyar's advisory capabilities, they begin referring their own clients to Boyar for complex structuring needs that exceed their local expertise. This referral dynamic reverses the typical TCSP model and creates an inbound deal flow channel with zero marketing cost. If the Network enables just 20 cross-border mandates per year at an average of $15K each, that's $300K in incremental revenue from a network that costs effectively nothing beyond relationship maintenance.
Single-vertical: $18K 3yr LTV. Multi-vertical: $69K 3yr LTV. The same client is worth 3.8x more — at zero incremental acquisition cost.

The Multi-Vertical Architecture is Boyar's structural response to the fundamental economics of TCSP advisory: client acquisition is expensive, but cross-selling to existing clients is nearly free. Boyar operates across six service verticals: Company Formation and Structuring, Corporate Services and Administration, Regulatory Licensing, Banking Facilitation, Trust and Estate Planning, and Fund Administration. Each vertical can independently acquire and serve clients, but the compounding economics happen when a client engages across multiple verticals.

A client with a BVI holding company, a UAE operating entity, a Singapore trust, a VASP license in Lithuania, and banking introductions in Switzerland — all managed through Boyar — would need to engage six different providers to replicate this relationship. The institutional knowledge is impossible to transfer. Once a client is engaged across 3+ verticals, the switching cost becomes prohibitive — moving to a competitor would require transferring corporate administration, regulatory filings, banking relationships, and compliance monitoring simultaneously, a disruption that most clients will not undertake unless the alternative firm offers dramatically superior service. The difference between 100 single-vertical clients and 100 multi-vertical clients: $1.8M versus $6.9M in three-year lifetime value from the same number of client relationships.
Remove any one moat and the system still works. Together, they create a compounding machine where each component amplifies every other component.

The most powerful aspect isn't any single moat — it's the interaction. The Advisory Moat surfaces cross-sell opportunities that expand wallet share. The Relationship Moat builds trust that makes clients comfortable adding verticals. The Licensing Cascade naturally generates corporate services, banking, and compliance engagements across multiple moats. The Experience Moat makes multi-jurisdictional delivery seamless. The Renewal Flywheel creates the structured touchpoints where cross-sell happens organically. And the Network enables the geographic reach that makes multi-jurisdictional client relationships possible in the first place. Remove any one and the system still works. Together, they create a compounding machine where each client relationship becomes more valuable over time, each jurisdiction deepens the network, each licensing mandate generates cascading revenue, and each renewal strengthens the recurring base.

Boyar isn't building a service firm with multiple revenue lines. It's building an interlocking system where each component amplifies the others. By Year 5–7, the combination and integration of all seven moats creates something that takes a decade to build from scratch.

Advisory Moat surfaces cross-sell → activates Wallet Share Moat. Relationship Moat builds trust → clients add verticals → compounds Wallet Share. Licensing Moat cascade generates formation + banking + compliance → activates Advisory + Renewal Flywheels. Experience Moat drives seamless delivery → reduces churn → strengthens Renewal Flywheel. Renewal Flywheel creates structured touchpoints → surfaces cross-sell → re-activates Advisory Moat. Boyar Network enables geographic reach → multi-jurisdictional delivery → activates all six simultaneously. The system is self-reinforcing. Every client engagement feeds multiple moats simultaneously. This is the essence of what takes legacy firms 20–30 years to build — and what Boyar is building from the first client engagement.
What Boyar Will Be Known For

A modern advisory firm that combines the depth of a traditional TCSP with the data infrastructure and client experience of a technology-enabled platform. Not a hockey stick — a compound curve. The kind that looks modest in Year 1, impressive by Year 3, and inevitable by Year 7.

Experience Moat Digital-Native, Next-Gen Ready 81% of HNWI inheritors plan to switch firms. Boyar is built for next-gen expectations from day one — the legacy conversion window takes 3–5 years. Inheritors Switching 81% Wealth Transfer $83.5T over 20 years Legacy Conversion Timeline 3–5 years Boyar's Advantage Window Open now Deep Dive The Experience Moat addresses a structural shift in client expectations. Next-generation wealth holders (millennials and Gen Z inheritors managing $83.5 trillion in transferred wealth) expect advisory services delivered with the same quality of digital experience they receive from consumer technology companies. Legacy TCSPs — operating on paper files, manual processes, and email-only communication — are structurally unable to meet these expectations without multi-million-dollar technology transformations. Boyar is built digital-native from inception: structured data pipelines, real-time client reporting, digital document management, and responsive multi-channel communication. The experience moat compounds as client expectations continue to rise. Every year, the gap between what next-gen clients expect and what legacy TCSPs deliver widens. Boyar's technology-forward approach means the firm can adopt new tools and platforms (AI-assisted compliance monitoring, automated regulatory reporting, client communication platforms) without the legacy-system integration burden that slows Tier 3 competitors. The full transformation of a legacy TCSP to digital delivery takes 3–5 years at institutional scale. During that window, Boyar owns the experience advantage.

Renewal Flywheel Compounding Revenue Moat 73 retained entities by Year 5 generating $128K+ in annual recurring revenue at 90%+ gross margin — before trust fees, corporate retainers, fund admin, or licensing compliance. Year 2 Renewals $21K recurring Year 3 Renewals $56K recurring Year 4 Renewals $91K recurring Year 5 Renewals $128K+ recurring Deep Dive The Renewal Flywheel is the mathematical proof of Boyar's compounding model. Every entity formed, every structure established, every license obtained generates recurring annual revenue: registered office fees, annual filings, compliance monitoring, corporate secretarial services, and regulatory reporting. By Year 5, the projected entity base is 73 active entities under administration. Each entity generates $1,750–$3,500 in annual recurring revenue. At 90%+ gross margin, this creates a revenue floor of $128K+ annually that compounds as each new year adds more entities to the base. The renewal flywheel is not automatic — it requires a deliberate retention process. Every Company Formation client gets a 90-day post-formation check-in, a 6-month review, and a 10-month renewal conversation. The cross-sell happens naturally in these touchpoints — a client who formed a company in UAE mentions they're now looking at Singapore, or needs a trust for family assets, or their startup just closed a seed round and the holding structure needs restructuring for the new cap table. The renewal isn't just an invoice — it's a relationship maintenance cycle that generates organic cross-sell at zero additional acquisition cost. By Year 5, total recurring revenue (including trust fees, corporate retainers, fund admin fees, and licensing compliance) should represent 55–65% of all revenue.

Boyar Network Geographic Moat 100+ vetted partners across 53 jurisdictions. Building a quality network takes 3–5 years. A new entrant cannot replicate it from scratch. Target Partners 100+ Jurisdictions 53 Incremental Revenue $300K/year at 20 mandates Network Build Time 3–5 years Deep Dive The Boyar Network is a curated ecosystem of vetted professional service partners — law firms, accounting firms, registered agents, compliance consultants, and banking introducers — spanning 53 jurisdictions worldwide. Unlike franchise networks or affiliate programs, the Boyar Network is built on bilateral quality standards: every partner is vetted against Boyar's compliance criteria (AML/CFT procedures, professional indemnity insurance, regulatory standing, reference checks), and every partner's work is quality-reviewed by Boyar before delivery to the end client. The network creates a geographic moat: a new entrant attempting to replicate Boyar's multi-jurisdictional capability would need to identify, vet, negotiate terms with, and operationally integrate 100+ partners across 53 jurisdictions — a process that takes years of active relationship building. The network also generates deal flow: as network partners become familiar with Boyar's advisory capabilities, they begin referring their own clients to Boyar for complex structuring needs that exceed their local expertise. This referral dynamic reverses the typical TCSP model and creates an inbound deal flow channel with zero marketing cost. If the Network enables just 20 cross-border mandates per year at an average of $15K each, that's $300K in incremental revenue from a network that costs effectively nothing beyond relationship maintenance.

Multi-Vertical Architecture Wallet Share Moat Single-vertical: $18K 3yr LTV. Multi-vertical: $69K 3yr LTV. The same client is worth 3.8x more — at zero incremental acquisition cost. Single-vertical LTV ~$18K Multi-vertical LTV ~$69K Retention at 4+ services >95% Retention at 1 service 70–75% Deep Dive The Multi-Vertical Architecture is Boyar's structural response to the fundamental economics of TCSP advisory: client acquisition is expensive, but cross-selling to existing clients is nearly free. Boyar operates across six service verticals: Company Formation and Structuring, Corporate Services and Administration, Regulatory Licensing, Banking Facilitation, Trust and Estate Planning, and Fund Administration. Each vertical can independently acquire and serve clients, but the compounding economics happen when a client engages across multiple verticals. A client with a BVI holding company, a UAE operating entity, a Singapore trust, a VASP license in Lithuania, and banking introductions in Switzerland — all managed through Boyar — would need to engage six different providers to replicate this relationship. The institutional knowledge is impossible to transfer. Once a client is engaged across 3+ verticals, the switching cost becomes prohibitive — moving to a competitor would require transferring corporate administration, regulatory filings, banking relationships, and compliance monitoring simultaneously, a disruption that most clients will not undertake unless the alternative firm offers dramatically superior service. The difference between 100 single-vertical clients and 100 multi-vertical clients: $1.8M versus $6.9M in three-year lifetime value from the same number of client relationships.

The Compound System Remove any one moat and the system still works. Together, they create a compounding machine where each component amplifies every other component. How the Moats Interact The most powerful aspect isn't any single moat — it's the interaction. The Advisory Moat surfaces cross-sell opportunities that expand wallet share. The Relationship Moat builds trust that makes clients comfortable adding verticals. The Licensing Cascade naturally generates corporate services, banking, and compliance engagements across multiple moats. The Experience Moat makes multi-jurisdictional delivery seamless. The Renewal Flywheel creates the structured touchpoints where cross-sell happens organically. And the Network enables the geographic reach that makes multi-jurisdictional client relationships possible in the first place. Remove any one and the system still works. Together, they create a compounding machine where each client relationship becomes more valuable over time, each jurisdiction deepens the network, each licensing mandate generates cascading revenue, and each renewal strengthens the recurring base. Boyar isn't building a service firm with multiple revenue lines. It's building an interlocking system where each component amplifies the others. By Year 5–7, the combination and integration of all seven moats creates something that takes a decade to build from scratch. The moat interaction map. Advisory Moat surfaces cross-sell → activates Wallet Share Moat. Relationship Moat builds trust → clients add verticals → compounds Wallet Share. Licensing Moat cascade generates formation + banking + compliance → activates Advisory + Renewal Flywheels. Experience Moat drives seamless delivery → reduces churn → strengthens Renewal Flywheel. Renewal Flywheel creates structured touchpoints → surfaces cross-sell → re-activates Advisory Moat. Boyar Network enables geographic reach → multi-jurisdictional delivery → activates all six simultaneously. The system is self-reinforcing. Every client engagement feeds multiple moats simultaneously. This is the essence of what takes legacy firms 20–30 years to build — and what Boyar is building from the first client engagement. What Boyar Will Be Known For A modern advisory firm that combines the depth of a traditional TCSP with the data infrastructure and client experience of a technology-enabled platform. Not a hockey stick — a compound curve. The kind that looks modest in Year 1, impressive by Year 3, and inevitable by Year 7.

/lib/competitive-data/risks.name: Lib > Competitive Data > Risks
content: All client relationships, business development, and institutional knowledge reside with the founder in Year 1–2. The most immediate execution risk.

The single-founder model is a deliberate Year 1–2 design choice, not an oversight. The constraint on scale forces discipline in client selection — every mandate must be a reference case. Specific mitigants: (1) Phased hiring plan — first associate in Year 2 when revenue triggers justify it, structured team by Year 3. (2) Deliberate pacing — client acquisition is limited to match execution capacity, preventing quality degradation. (3) Process documentation — every client workflow is documented in sufficient detail that a trained associate can execute it. (4) Key person insurance secured in Year 1. (5) Boyar Network partner firms can absorb client administration if the founder is temporarily unavailable. The goal is to make the founder's personal involvement a quality differentiator in Year 1, not a single point of failure by Year 3. By mid-Year 2, the first senior hire independently manages 30–40% of relationships. All structuring documentation and relationship histories are systematically captured.
The MiCA deadline has already been subject to national transitional extensions. A deferral shifts — but does not eliminate — licensing demand.

MiCA enforcement is already in progress — the regulation entered into force in June 2023, with CASP authorization requirements taking effect July 1, 2026. While transition periods could be extended, the regulatory infrastructure is deployed and irreversible. Specific mitigants: (1) Boyar's revenue model is not MiCA-dependent — formation, structuring, and corporate services generate baseline revenue independent of any single regulatory event. (2) Even if the MiCA deadline shifts by 6–12 months, the licensing demand doesn't disappear — it defers. Clients who need VASP authorization will need it eventually. (3) The licensing vertical is not mono-regulatory. iGaming licensing (Curacao new model, Malta Gaming Authority), EMI/MSB licensing, and forex licensing continue independently of MiCA timeline. Revenue projections never depend on a single regulatory catalyst. The worst-case scenario: MiCA licensing revenue shifts from Year 2 to Year 3, reducing Year 2 revenue by $150K–$300K but not threatening the firm's viability.
In Year 1, the top 3 clients could represent 50–60% of revenue. Concentration risk is a mathematical inevitability of early stage — managed through deliberate diversification.

Client concentration is a mathematical inevitability in Year 1–2 (small client base, high-value mandates). Specific mitigants: (1) Target no single client exceeding 15% of annual revenue by Year 3, and 10% by Year 5. (2) Actively diversify the pipeline across service lines (formation, structuring, licensing, corporate services) and client segments (HNWI families, crypto firms, traditional corporates). The paid media experiment in Year 1 deliberately targets 5 distinct regions to ensure pipeline diversification from the outset. (3) Build recurring revenue (corporate services renewals) that provides a diversified revenue base independent of any single mandate — by Year 3, renewals from 22+ entities represent $56K in recurring revenue at zero concentration risk. (4) Maintain pipeline discipline — even when a large mandate is tempting, ensure that smaller mandates continue to flow to prevent concentration creep. The renewal flywheel naturally dilutes concentration as the client base grows.
Partner banks may change policies, exit client segments, or terminate TCSP relationships with minimal notice. Banking access is the most fragile link in the value chain.

Banking relationships are the most fragile link in the TCSP value chain. Banks may change policies, exit client segments, increase due diligence requirements, or terminate TCSP relationships with minimal notice. Specific mitigants: (1) Maintain 3–5 banking relationships per key jurisdiction — no single banking partner should be a bottleneck for any client type or jurisdiction. (2) Build the Boyar Network's banking referral capacity so that banking facilitation is distributed across multiple network partners, not concentrated in Boyar's direct relationships. (3) Develop relationships with digital banks and fintech banking platforms (EMI-licensed institutions, neo-banks for corporates) that are more receptive to TCSP-introduced clients and operate with faster onboarding timelines. (4) Provide banking partners with consistently high-quality due diligence packages, reducing their compliance burden and making Boyar a preferred introduction source rather than a generic agent. The licensing vertical strengthens banking access — a licensed VASP is easier to bank than an unlicensed one, and completed licensing mandates become the primary reference for banking partner relationships.
TMF, Vistra, or IQ-EQ could launch boutique tiers targeting mid-market clients. Large platforms structurally cannot replicate boutique attention.

Competitive threats come from two directions: Tier 1 mass incorporators moving upmarket into advisory structuring, and Tier 3 legacy firms investing in digital delivery and licensing capability. Specific mitigants: (1) The advisory moat — genuine advisory conversion (30% of formation inquiries to full structures) requires expertise and credibility that cannot be bought or quickly built. The knowledge compounds with each completed mandate. (2) The licensing moat — MiCA/VASP licensing capability requires deep regulatory knowledge that takes years of mandate experience to develop. A competitor entering in 2028 needs 2–3 years to reach Boyar's depth. (3) The relationship moat — founder-led client relationships with direct access to senior decision-makers cannot be replicated by institutional firms with rotating relationship managers. (4) Speed advantage — by the time competitors recognize and respond to Boyar's positioning, the firm will have 3–5 years of executed mandates, established relationships, and compounding brand equity. Large platforms structurally cannot replicate boutique attention: their cost structures make it uneconomical to service $30K–$75K mandates with depth. Sovereign has coexisted with Vistra for decades because this segment prefers personal service.
A major jurisdiction could change its tax regime or substance requirements. Every restructuring triggered by regulatory change is itself a billable engagement.

Regulatory risk is bidirectional: increased enforcement creates advisory demand (positive for Boyar), while regulatory relaxation could reduce compliance obligations and advisory budgets (negative). Specific mitigants: (1) Boyar's advisory model is regulation-agnostic — the firm helps clients comply with whatever framework applies, rather than betting on any specific regulatory outcome. (2) The trend is unidirectional toward more regulation, more categories, and more compliance requirements. Even in jurisdictions that relax specific rules, the overall compliance surface area continues to expand. (3) The 53-jurisdiction coverage is designed for regulatory resilience. No single jurisdiction exceeds 15% of revenue by Year 3. Every restructuring triggered by regulatory change in any jurisdiction is itself a billable engagement — clients need new structures, new compliance frameworks, and new banking relationships when jurisdictions change their rules. (4) When a jurisdiction changes, Boyar's clients need to restructure. That restructuring is Boyar's mandate. Regulatory change is not a threat to the business model — it is a demand generator.

/revenue/banking-projection.name: Banking Revenue Projection EMI Commission Scenarios
content: Banking Revenue — EMI Commission Scenarios. Passive referral commission by client risk tier.

Boyar earns passive EMI referral commission by introducing clients to Electronic Money Institutions. Boyar is the introducer, not the processor. Zero operational cost, zero regulatory exposure. The EMI processes transactions and holds funds. Boyar earns commission for the introduction. Pure margin, permanently recurring.

EMI Tier 1 — Small fintech / SaaS client. Risk: LOW. Monthly EMI volume: $50,000. Annual volume: $600,000. Commission rate: 0.02% (20 bps). Annual commission per client: $1,200. Monthly commission: $100. EMI own fee: 0.5–1%. Boyar share of EMI fee: ~25%. Profile: Seed–Series A SaaS, digital nomad agency, e-com brand. Why this rate: Low-risk flows, thin EMI margin, small referral share. Why EMI: Multi-currency payouts, instant SEPA, no bank friction. Stickiness: Medium — integrated into invoicing. Bank access: Easy. EMI dependency: Optional.

EMI Tier 2 — Mid-tier corporate client. Risk: LOW–MED. Monthly EMI volume: $100,000. Annual volume: $1,200,000. Commission rate: 0.03% (30 bps). Annual commission per client: $3,600. Monthly commission: $300. EMI own fee: 0.5–1.5%. Boyar share of EMI fee: ~25%. Profile: TaaS, KPO, EdTech, offshore holding $5M–$20M billing. Why this rate: Higher volume tier, cross-border SWIFT+SEPA adds EMI margin. Why EMI: IBAN issuance, multi-entity treasury, mid-market FX. Stickiness: Very high — 3–5yr IBAN lock-in with suppliers. Bank access: Moderate. EMI dependency: Preferred.

EMI Tier 3 — Forex broker client. Risk: HIGH. Monthly EMI volume: $500,000. Annual volume: $6,000,000. Commission rate: 0.06% (60 bps). Annual commission per client: $36,000. Monthly commission: $3,000. EMI own fee: 1.5–3%. Boyar share of EMI fee: ~30%. Profile: Offshore broker (Vanuatu, Seychelles, BVI). Why this rate: EMIs charge brokers 1.5–3%. Boyar gets ~30% referral cut. Why EMI: Banks will not touch FX brokers. Skrill/Neteller = industry standard. Stickiness: Extreme — switching = losing depositors. Bank access: Hard. EMI dependency: Required.

EMI Tier 4 — iGaming operator client. Risk: VERY HIGH. Monthly EMI volume: $2,080,000. Annual volume: $25,000,000. Commission rate: 0.08% (80 bps). Annual commission per client: $200,000. Monthly commission: $16,667. EMI own fee: 2–5%. Boyar share of EMI fee: ~25%. Profile: Curacao/MGA-licensed casino, sportsbook, poker. Why this rate: iGaming = highest EMI fees. Paysafe charges 2–5% on deposits. Why EMI: Regulatory mandate — MGA: 12.4% deposits, 25%+ withdrawals via e-wallets. Stickiness: Permanent — regulatory infrastructure, not a choice. Bank access: Very hard. EMI dependency: Mandated.

EMI Tier 5 — Crypto / VASP client. Risk: VERY HIGH. Monthly EMI volume: $2,080,000. Annual volume: $25,000,000. Commission rate: 0.10% (100 bps). Annual commission per client: $250,000. Monthly commission: $20,833. EMI own fee: 1.5–4%. Boyar share of EMI fee: ~35%. Profile: Mid-tier exchange, EU/UK fiat rails. Why this rate: Peak EMI pricing. On/off-ramp fees 1.5–4%. Top referral bracket. Why EMI: No alternative. Binance, Kraken, Gemini all confirmed EMI-dependent. Stickiness: Operational lifeline — EMI is how users deposit/withdraw fiat. Bank access: Near impossible. EMI dependency: Existential.

BPS means basis points. 1 bps = 0.01%. So 20 bps = 0.20%, 30 bps = 0.30%, 60 bps = 0.60%, 80 bps = 0.80%, 100 bps = 1.00%. For a SaaS client, Boyar earns 20 bps (0.02%) commission on EMI volume. For a crypto/VASP client, Boyar earns 100 bps (1.00%) commission.

How many bps commission for a SaaS client? 20 bps (0.02%). For a mid-tier corporate? 30 bps (0.03%). For a forex broker? 60 bps (0.06%). For an iGaming operator? 80 bps (0.08%). For a crypto/VASP? 100 bps (1.00%).
208x gap between lowest and highest tier. One iGaming or crypto client generates more passive income than the entire SaaS portfolio combined. Commission scales with risk and volume — not effort.

Higher risk = higher EMI fees = higher referral cut. EMIs charge 0.5–1% for SaaS, 1.5–3% for forex, 2–5% for iGaming. Boyar referral cut is ~25–35% of the EMI own fee. The rate mechanically scales with risk tier.
Bank rejection drives EMI dependency. Traditional banks reject forex, iGaming, and crypto. These sectors use EMIs because there is no other fiat rail. Structural lock-in means zero voluntary churn.

$25M/yr volume is mid-tier for gaming and crypto. Paysafe processed $167B in 2025. A single mid-tier exchange or casino doing $25M/yr is a rounding error for the EMI but a transformative referral for Boyar.
Portfolio Mix A — SaaS-heavy: 5 SaaS, 3 mid-tier, 2 forex, 0 iGaming, 0 crypto. 10 clients total. Annual commission: $84,000.
Portfolio Mix B — Balanced: 3 SaaS, 3 mid-tier, 2 forex, 1 iGaming, 1 crypto. 10 clients total. Annual commission: $535,400.
Portfolio Mix C — High-risk weighted: 1 SaaS, 2 mid-tier, 3 forex, 2 iGaming, 2 crypto. 10 clients total. Annual commission: $1,016,400.

All three portfolios have exactly 10 clients. The 8.5x revenue gap ($84,000 vs $1,016,400) comes entirely from mix. Every formation client in crypto, forex, or iGaming that Boyar routes to an EMI partner converts a one-time $6,500 banking fee into a compounding passive stream worth $36K–$250K per year. The banking fee is the introduction. The EMI commission is the business model.
Comparison table — clients needed for $36K/yr: SaaS needs 30 clients, mid-tier corporate needs 10 clients, forex broker needs 1 client, iGaming needs 0.18 clients, crypto/VASP needs 0.14 clients.

/revenue/licensing-projection.name: Licensing Revenue Projection
content: Licensing Revenue Projection — Five year outlook for Boyar Partners.

Four licensing tiers: Crypto/CASP (45% weight, $12,000 fee, $4,000 renewal), Forex/Securities (25% weight, $18,000 fee, $6,000 renewal), Banking (10% weight, $35,000 fee, $15,000 renewal), Fund/Gaming (20% weight, $20,000 fee, $5,000 renewal).
Blended new client fee: $17,400 (tier-weighted from 14 proposals). Blended renewal fee: $5,800 per year. Renewal rate: 55%.

Year 1: 0 new clients, $0 revenue. Year 1 focuses on deploying funds to acquire 16 clients across six core services. Licensing engagements run 3–12 months from proposal to delivered license. Year 1 builds pipeline, not fee recognition.
Year 2: 2 new clients, $34,800 new revenue, 0 renewals, $0 renewal revenue. Total: $34,800. Cumulative: $34,800.
Year 3: 3 new clients, $52,200 new revenue, 1 renewal, $5,800 renewal revenue. Total: $58,000. Cumulative: $92,800.
Year 4: 4 new clients, $69,600 new revenue, 2 renewals, $11,600 renewal revenue. Total: $81,200. Cumulative: $174,000.
Year 5: 5 new clients, $87,000 new revenue, 3 renewals, $17,400 renewal revenue. Total: $104,400. Cumulative: $278,400.
Five year cumulative licensing revenue: $278,400 from 14 new clients plus renewals.
Y5 licensing share of combined revenue: 13.4% of combined $777,140. Core 6 services revenue by year: Y1 $111,900, Y2 $212,780, Y3 $315,500, Y4 $539,970, Y5 $672,740.

Sensitivity analysis — Bear case: clients 0,1,2,3,3 at $14,000 fee, 40% renewal rate. Five year cumulative: $136,800 (-51% vs base). Base case: clients 0,2,3,4,5 at $17,400 fee, 55% renewal rate. Five year cumulative: $278,400 (reference). Bull case: clients 1,3,5,6,7 at $21,000 fee, 65% renewal rate. Five year cumulative: $543,200 (+95% vs base).

Bear case assumes MiCA demand cools, crypto winter extends, and only forex and fund clients convert. Bull case assumes one banking client at $35,000 per year and higher cross sell from MiCA driven CASP demand.
MiCA is creating unprecedented demand. Over 40 CASP licenses have been issued across EU member states since December 2024. Every existing virtual asset provider must apply again by July 2026.
Fulfillment partners have already delivered more than 130 licenses. Primary partner Manimama delivered 130+ licenses globally. Gatwick Law (established 1995, UAE) gives a second fulfillment channel.
This model carries zero incremental CAC. Licensing keywords are already in the content strategy. Clients arrive through cross sell, inbound content, and paid traffic already budgeted.
Revenue is stated gross rather than net margin. Boyar outsources ~80% of work to partners and retains 20–35% as advisory and coordination margin.

What happens if licensing does not materialise? The five year core revenue stack without licensing already reaches $672,740 by Year 5. Licensing at $104,400 is a 13.4% uplift — attractive but not load bearing.

/compliance/advertising-eligibility.name: Digital Advertising Compliance & Platform Eligibility
content: Boyar Partners is fully eligible to run paid advertising across Google, YouTube, Meta (Facebook & Instagram), and LinkedIn.

Boyar Partners is a Trust & Corporate Services Provider (TCSP). It does not provide financial products, financial advice, investment management, lending, insurance, or any service that involves the management or investment of client funds.
Boyar Partners is classified as Professional / Business Services on every advertising platform — NOT as a Financial Services advertiser.

The service portfolio includes: company formation and incorporation, corporate structuring and multi-entity architecture, trust establishment and administration, registered office and nominee services, banking introduction facilitation (introductions only — not banking products), regulatory licensing advisory (VASP, iGaming, EMI — application facilitation, not the licence itself), fund administration support, citizenship and residency pathway advisory.

Google Ads (Search, Display & YouTube): Boyar Partners is ELIGIBLE. Classified as Professional / Business Services, NOT Financial Services. Only standard Google Advertiser Verification is required. The Financial Services Verification (FSV) programme does not apply. No prohibited content categories apply. One caution: CBI/residency ads must be framed as advisory and facilitation, never as direct provision of passports or visas.

Google defines financial products and services as products and services related to the management or investment of money and cryptocurrencies, including personalized advice. Boyar Partners does not manage money, offer investment products, or provide personalized financial advice.
Google compliant language: Residency & citizenship pathway advisory, Expert guidance on investment migration programmes. Not acceptable: Get your second passport, Buy citizenship in 90 days.

Meta (Facebook & Instagram): Boyar Partners is ELIGIBLE. Classified as Professional / Business Services, NOT Financial Products & Services. Standard Business Verification through Meta Business Manager is required. Financial Services Authorisation (FSA) is not mandatory but may be proactively applied for.

Meta's Special Ad Category for Financial Products and Services does NOT apply to Boyar Partners. This means full access to: Lookalike Audiences, detailed interest-based targeting, Custom Audiences, precise geo-targeting, age and demographic segmentation.

Meta's automated ad review system may over-flag ads using keywords such as trust, offshore, banking, nominee, and asset protection. These are legitimate in the context of corporate services. Mitigation strategies include language discipline and proactive compliance.

LinkedIn: Boyar Partners is ELIGIBLE. No restrictions apply. Cleanest compliance path of all platforms. Standard LinkedIn advertiser account setup required. Full targeting capabilities available: job title and seniority targeting, industry and company size filtering, geographic targeting, company name targeting for ABM strategies, interest and group-based targeting.
LinkedIn restriction: cannot target by income bracket directly. Workaround: use seniority, job title, and company size proxies which are more precise for our client profile.

Operational safeguards for advertising compliance: Language discipline — use terms like international company formation, cross-border corporate structuring, entity management, corporate administration, trust establishment, regulatory licensing advisory, residency pathway advisory, banking introduction facilitation.

Terms to avoid or contextualise carefully in ads: offshore (use international or cross-border), shell company, tax avoidance, second passport, buy citizenship, guaranteed approval, anonymous, hidden, secret.

Landing page compliance requirements: display registered business name and physical office address, clear description of service, TCSP licence details and jurisdictional registrations, HTTPS security, privacy policy and terms of engagement, no misleading claims or guarantees of outcomes.

All advertising accounts will be set up using verified business entities through each platform's Business Manager. Ad creative will be reviewed internally before submission. Appeal submissions within 48 hours of any automated rejection. Monthly compliance reporting in board reviews.
Regional compliance: GDPR-compliant data handling for EU campaigns, CAN-SPAM and CCPA compliance for US campaigns, PDPA compliance for Southeast Asian campaigns.

Year 1 marketing budget allocates $17,000 in total ad spend across all platforms. Regional allocation: Europe 35% ($6,000) via Google and LinkedIn, Asia & MENA 30% ($5,143) via Google and Meta, North America 25% ($4,286) via LinkedIn and Google, South Africa 5% ($857) via Meta and Google, South America 5% ($857) via Meta.
This spend level is well below the thresholds that trigger enhanced platform scrutiny. Combined with the non-financial-services classification, the risk of account-level restrictions is minimal.

Platform eligibility summary: Google (Search & Display) — Eligible, Professional Services, Standard Advertiser Verification, no FSV required. YouTube — Eligible, Professional Services, same as Google Ads. Meta (Facebook & Instagram) — Eligible, Professional Services, Standard Business Verification, no Special Ad Category. LinkedIn — Eligible, Professional Services, Standard Account Setup, no restrictions.
Boyar Partners is not subject to heightened restrictions, special ad categories, or mandatory financial services verification processes that apply to financial product advertisers.

Can Boyar Partners run ads legally? Yes. Boyar Partners is fully eligible to run paid digital advertising across Google, YouTube, Meta, and LinkedIn. The firm is classified as a professional corporate and legal facilitation services provider, not a financial services advertiser.
The advertising compliance document is reviewed and updated quarterly, or immediately upon any material change to platform advertising policies.
